common_name: Simpson Okra (1940s Tennessee Heirloom Spineless-Type Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed past 70°F; soaking seed overnight speeds germination in Simpson's slightly slower-sprouting seed coat.

directions: Keep pods picked every day or two once they reach 3 inches, since Simpson's smooth, straight pods pass from tender to woody faster than many longer-podded types. The family lineage traces to the Simpson household in Rogersville, Tennessee, where it was grown and passed down at least since the 1940s, giving it a straight, light-green pod very similar in appearance to Clemson Spineless. Plants tolerate the heat and dry spells of a Gulf Coast August with little complaint, continuing to set pods as long as harvest stays current. Because it is open-pollinated, gardeners can save seed from dried pods left on the plant at season's end for replanting the following year.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange
Sandhill Preservation Center

common_name: Jefferson Okra (University of Arkansas Early Semi-Dwarf Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed and soil is reliably warm; Jefferson's early maturity means a Gulf Coast gardener can often squeeze in a second planting in early summer.

directions: Space plants a bit closer than tall heirloom types since Jefferson's semi-dwarf, sparsely branched habit takes up less garden footprint while still producing a full-season crop. Bred in the University of Arkansas horticulture program from a cross involving Clemson Spineless, Emerald, Perkins, Gold Coast, and other parent lines, Jefferson was selected to mature roughly ten days ahead of Clemson Spineless, giving an earlier start to the harvest window in a warm Gulf South spring. Pods are straight, dark green, and ribbed with few spines, making them easy to handle during the frequent picking okra demands. Because the plants stay relatively compact, Jefferson also works well in a raised bed or smaller garden plot where a 6-foot okra stand would crowd out neighboring crops.

common_name: Hernandez Sweet Potato (1992 LSU AgCenter Disease-Resistant Orange Sweet Potato)

planting.note: Set rooted slips after the last frost once soil has warmed well past 65°F, planting into loose, well-drained, mounded rows; sandy loam soils bring out Hernandez's best root shape.

directions: Plant slips into ridged, sandy-loam rows for the smoothest, most uniform roots, since Hernandez performs best where drainage is quick and soil is loose rather than heavy clay. Released by the LSU AgCenter sweet potato breeding program in 1992 under breeder Don La Bonte, Hernandez carries reddish-brown skin over deep orange, smooth, string-free flesh with a mild, sweet flavor that holds up well whether baked or boiled. The variety was bred for resistance to fusarium wilt, root-knot nematodes, soil rot, and internal cork, which makes it a dependable, low-input choice for a Gulf Coast garden bed that has grown sweet potatoes before. Cure roots in a warm, humid spot for one to two weeks after harvest to set the skin and sweeten the flesh before long-term storage.

common_name: Bienville Sweet Potato (2002 LSU AgCenter Patented Nematode-Resistant Sweet Potato)

planting.note: Set slips after last frost into warm, sandy-loam, well-drained ridges; Bienville was bred for exactly this kind of lighter-textured soil common across the Gulf Coast's sandier parishes and counties.

directions: Grow Bienville much as you would its close relative Beauregard, since the two orange-fleshed varieties are nearly identical at the table; Bienville's main advantage is its stronger resistance to southern root-knot nematode, the soil pest that plagues light, sandy ground. Released by the LSU AgCenter in 2002 and awarded a U.S. plant patent, Bienville was developed by breeder Don La Bonte specifically to give growers in nematode-prone sandy-loam parishes a lower-input alternative to standard commercial types. Vines are vigorous and sprawling, so allow generous row spacing or let them run into surrounding open ground. Harvest before the first fall cold snap and cure roots in a warm, humid location for about a week to improve storage life and sweetness.

common_name: Resisto Sweet Potato (Classic Multi-State Disease-Resistant Copper Sweet Potato)

planting.note: Set slips into warm, well-drained ridges after all frost danger passes; Resisto's broad disease resistance makes it forgiving of garden beds with a history of soil-borne sweet potato problems.

directions: Choose Resisto for a bed where previous sweet potato crops have struggled with soil insects or disease, since it was bred specifically for a broad combination of resistances rather than for any single standout trait. Developed jointly by the USDA and the South Carolina and Texas Agricultural Experiment Stations as a seedling selection from the older W-56 line, Resisto produces reddish-copper skin over dark orange flesh with notably high beta-carotene content and roots that store and can well. Vines are vigorous and open-pollinated, performing reliably across a wide range of Southern soils and summers. Cure roots in a warm, humid spot for about a week after digging to heal skin nicks and concentrate sweetness before moving them to long-term storage.

common_name: Allgold Sweet Potato (1952 Oklahoma State Vining Orange Sweet Potato)

planting.note: Set slips into warm, loose, well-drained soil after the last frost; Allgold's long vigorous vines need generous room to sprawl across the bed or into a pathway.

directions: Give Allgold's vigorous, far-ranging vines plenty of room, since this older variety was selected for heavy yield rather than a compact habit. Introduced in 1952 by Oklahoma State from a cross of the Creole and Triumph varieties, Allgold produces tan skin over orange flesh and was valued in its day for consistently heavy production across a range of Southern growing conditions. It is a straightforward, old-fashioned baking type without the modern disease-resistance packages bred into newer releases, so rotate planting beds to avoid a buildup of soil-borne sweet potato pests. Cure harvested roots in a warm, humid spot for roughly a week to firm the skin and bring out the full sweetness before storing.

common_name: Elite Cream Cowpea (Heavy-Yielding Bush-Type Cream Southern Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed past 65°F and all frost danger has passed; Elite's early maturity allows a Gulf Coast gardener to fit in two or more successive sowings across a long summer.

directions: Direct sow in warm, lean to moderately fertile soil, avoiding heavy nitrogen fertilizer, which pushes foliage growth at the expense of pods. Elite is a compact, bush-type open-pollinated cream southern pea prized among market growers and home gardeners for being among the heaviest-yielding of all the cream-type cowpeas, producing abundant 7-inch pods that shell easily. The small, pale cream peas cook up light in color and mild in flavor, making a classic side dish alongside cornbread. Like all cowpeas, Elite fixes nitrogen in the soil as it grows and thrives in the peak summer heat that stalls cooler-season legumes, making it a reliable, low-input crop for Gulf South vegetable gardens.

common_name: Pinkeye Purple Hull BVR Cowpea (1984 University of Georgia Virus-Resistant Purple Hull Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep once soil has warmed past 65°F; BVR's resistance to blackeye cowpea mosaic virus makes it a safer choice where that disease has shown up in previous seasons.

directions: Direct sow in full sun after the soil has warmed, spacing plants to allow good air movement, which helps keep foliage disease in check even though BVR already carries built-in virus resistance. Selected at the University of Georgia in Athens from the classic Pinkeye Purple Hull and released in 1984, this bush-to-semi-vining type was bred specifically for resistance to blackeye cowpea mosaic virus, a problem that can stunt and discolor susceptible cowpea plantings. Pods set up above the foliage for easy picking and start out green before coloring to the familiar rosy-purple hull, with the peas themselves turning cream with a distinctive maroon pink eye. Pick pods at the green-shell stage for the mildest flavor, or let them dry fully on the vine for long-keeping dried peas.

common_name: Mississippi Pinkeye 2 Purplehull Cowpea (Patented Cold-Tolerant Improved Purple Hull Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow a bit earlier in the window than most cowpeas, since this cultivar was specifically improved for stronger seedling emergence and cold tolerance in cooler early-season soil.

directions: Take advantage of this variety's improved cold tolerance by sowing it slightly earlier in spring than standard Mississippi Pinkeye Purple Hull, since breeding work focused on stronger emergence and seedling survival in cooler soil. Covered by a U.S. plant patent as an improved selection of the older Mississippi Pinkeye Purple Hull, this cultivar reaches shelling stage in roughly 60 days, a few days ahead of its parent. Pods carry the classic purple hull color over pink-eyed cream peas with excellent flavor, equally good eaten fresh or dried for winter storage. Keep plantings picked regularly through the heat of summer, since consistent harvest keeps the compact bush setting new flushes of pods.

common_name: Carolina Cream Cowpea (Clemson-Associated Light-Cooking Cream Southern Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed past 65°F and frost danger has fully passed; this cream-type pea benefits from a slightly later start than blackeye types since it prefers consistently warm ground.

directions: Sow in full sun in warm, well-drained soil of moderate fertility, since cream peas like this one are prone to excess vine growth at the expense of pods in overly rich beds. Carolina Cream is a smaller-statured, light-seeded cream southern pea associated with Clemson University's long-running southern pea breeding program, which also produced well-known releases such as Zipper Cream and Colossus. The pale, cream-colored peas cook up with a notably light-colored pot liquor and mild, delicate flavor compared to the darker broth of crowder and field pea types. Harvest at the green-shell stage for the best fresh eating quality, picking every couple of days during peak summer production to keep plants setting new pods.

common_name: Texas Cream 12 Cowpea (1953 Texas A&M Disease-Resistant Bush Cream Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed past 65°F; Texas Cream 12's wilt and nematode resistance make it a dependable repeat crop in beds that have grown southern peas for several seasons.

directions: Direct sow in full sun in warm soil of moderate fertility, and expect a tidy, upright bush habit that stays easy to pick through the season. Released by the Texas Agricultural Experiment Station in 1953, Texas Cream 12 was bred for resistance to both fusarium wilt and root-knot nematode, two of the most persistent soil-borne threats to repeated southern pea plantings. Pods are greatly curved with slight constrictions between the attractive cream-colored peas, turning from green at fresh-shell stage to dark straw at the dry stage. The variety performs reliably through Gulf Coast summer heat and makes an excellent fresh shelling pea for market growers and home gardeners alike.

common_name: California Blackeye 46 Cowpea (1987 UC Davis Fusarium-Resistant Blackeye Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed past 65°F; CB46's two main flushes of pods come fairly close together, so plan harvest help for a concentrated picking window rather than a long trickle.

directions: Direct sow in full sun in warm, lean to moderately fertile soil, since this upright bush type is bred for compact, easy-to-harvest growth rather than sprawling vines. Developed and released in 1987 by the University of California, Davis, and the California Agricultural Experiment Station, California Blackeye 46 was bred for resistance to fusarium wilt races 1 and 2 as well as root-knot nematode, making it a dependable standard in fields and gardens with a history of those soil problems. Plants produce two concentrated flushes of well-filled 6 to 8 inch pods borne above the foliage, with classic cream-colored, black-eyed peas inside. Pick at the green-shell stage for fresh eating, or allow pods to dry fully for the traditional dried black-eyed pea used in Southern New Year's dishes.
